welcome: Learn science, engineering, technology and math the hands-on way. Read or listen to each lesson, play with the labs, build real projects, and earn your STEM Master certificate.

mods.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
mods.tag: Observe, sort, and think like a scientist
mods.intro: Every scientist — from lab researchers to bridge engineers — starts with the same tools: sharp eyes, good questions, and honest records. In this module you will train your senses, sort the world into groups, spot patterns, and run your first real experiment using the scientific method.
objs: Use all five senses to make careful observations.
Sort objects by their properties.
Find and extend patterns.
Follow the five steps of the scientific method.

lessons.title: Your Five Super-Senses
paras: Scientists observe with their five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.
A good observation describes exactly what you notice, not how you feel about it. "The leaf is green and waxy" is an observation. "The leaf is pretty" is an opinion.

Each sense catches different clues. Your eyes see color and shape. Your ears hear high and low sounds, and loud and soft ones. Your nose can warn you before your eyes do, like when you smell rain before a storm arrives. Your skin tells you if something is rough or smooth, hot or cold.
Safety rule: scientists never taste or touch unknown things. In a lab, you only use taste and touch when your teacher says it is safe.
lessons.try: Close your eyes. Have a partner hand you three objects. Describe each using touch alone — then open your eyes and check. How many properties did you get right?

lessons.title: Sorting the World
paras: Sorting means grouping things by a shared property: color, shape, size, texture, or what they are made of. When you sort your toys into bins, you are doing exactly what museum scientists do with fossils.
The property you choose is called the sorting rule. One collection can be sorted many ways — buttons can be sorted by color, by number of holes, or by size. Each rule shows you something different.
Engineers sort too. Builders sort materials: wood here, steel there, glass over there. Sorting keeps big projects organized.
lessons.try: Grab 20 small objects. Sort them by one rule, then re-sort the same objects by a different rule. Which rule was easiest? Which showed you something surprising?

lessons.title: Patterns Everywhere
paras: A pattern is anything that repeats in a regular way: red-blue-red-blue, or 2-4-6-8. Once you find the rule of a pattern, you can predict what comes next — and prediction is the heart of science.
Patterns hide in nature: the stripes on a tiger, the segments of a pinecone, day following night. They hide in buildings too: windows marching across a skyscraper in a perfect row.
Math patterns use numbers. In 5, 10, 15, 20, the rule is 'add 5.' The next number is 25. Finding rules in number patterns trains the same brain muscle engineers use to spot problems in data.
lessons.try: What comes next? 3, 6, 9, 12, __. Now make up your own number pattern and challenge a partner to find your rule.

lessons.title: The Scientific Method
paras: The scientific method is a five-step recipe for discovering truth: 1) Ask a QUESTION. 2) Make a HYPOTHESIS — a testable prediction. 3) TEST it with a fair experiment. 4) OBSERVE and record DATA. 5) Draw a CONCLUSION.

A fair test changes only ONE thing at a time. If you test whether ramp height affects car speed, you must use the same car and the same ramp surface every time — only the height changes. Everything else stays the same.

Here is the secret most people miss: a hypothesis that turns out wrong is still a success. You learned something true about the world. Scientists celebrate wrong predictions because each one points toward the right answer.
lessons.try: Question: does ice melt faster in sunlight or in shade? Write your hypothesis. Then test it with two ice cubes, one in each spot. Write down what you see every 5 minutes.

build.title: The Mystery Powder Lab
build.mission: Use observation and sorting to tell three mystery white powders apart — like a forensic scientist.
materials: Salt, sugar, and baking soda (labeled A, B, C by a grown-up)
Paper and pencil for your data table
steps: SAFETY FIRST: look and touch only. Do NOT taste anything.
Observe each powder with your eyes and the magnifier. Record color, grain size, and shape.
Rub a pinch between your fingers. Record how each feels.
Stir one spoonful of each into its own cup of water. Watch for 2 minutes. Record what happens.
Sort your observations into a table. Which powder is which? Write your conclusion and your evidence.
think: Which powder has the biggest grains?
Which one disappeared fastest in water?
Which two look most alike, and how did you tell them apart?
build.science: You just did real analytical science. Forensic labs identify unknown substances the same way: observe properties, run tests, compare results, and conclude based on evidence — never on guessing.

mods.title: Forces & Motion
mods.intro: Everything that moves does so because a force pushed or pulled it. In this module you will race cars down ramps, boss magnets around, and discover why some things float and others sink. Forces are invisible — but their effects are everywhere.
objs: Describe pushes and pulls as forces.
Explain how ramp height and friction change motion.
Predict what magnets will attract or repel.
Connect floating and sinking to density.

lessons.title: Pushes and Pulls
paras: A force is simply a push or a pull. Kicking a ball is a push. Opening a door is a pull. Every motion you have ever seen started with a force.

Bigger forces make bigger changes. A gentle push rolls a ball slowly; a hard kick sends it flying. The direction of the force decides the direction of the motion — push the swing from behind and it moves forward.
Engineers think in forces all day. When they design a bridge, they ask: which way will the wind push? How hard will traffic press down? Every structure is an answer to forces.
lessons.try: Roll a ball with a soft push, then a hard push. Measure how far each roll goes. What changed — and what stayed the same?

lessons.title: Friction and Ramps
paras: Friction is the force that fights sliding. Rough surfaces, like carpet, grab things and slow them down. Smooth surfaces, like ice, let things glide. That is why sleds zoom on snow but crawl on grass.
A ramp turns height into speed. Gravity pulls the car down the slope. A steeper ramp gives gravity a stronger pull, so the car goes faster and rolls farther.

Here is how to make it a fair test. To prove that height matters, keep the car, the ramp surface, and the way you let go exactly the same. Change ONLY the height. That is the scientific method from Module 1 in action!
lessons.try: Slide a book across carpet, then across a smooth floor. Which surface has more friction? How could you measure the difference?

lessons.title: Marvelous Magnets
paras: Magnets pull certain metals — iron and steel — toward them without touching. This invisible pull works through paper, water, and even your hand.
Every magnet has two poles: north and south. Opposite poles ATTRACT (pull together). Like poles REPEL (push apart). You can feel the repel force pushing back when you force two north poles together.
Magnets are engineering tools, not just toys. They hold cabinet doors shut, spin the motors in fans and electric cars, and let maglev trains float above their tracks.
lessons.try: Tape a paperclip to a string. Can you lift it with a magnet without touching it? Now try through a book. What blocks the pull — and what doesn't?

lessons.title: Sink or Float
paras: Whether something floats depends on density. Density means how much stuff is packed into a space. Things that are less dense than water float. Things that are more dense than water sink.
A giant steel ship floats because it is full of air. When you count the steel and all that air together, the ship is less dense than water.
Shape matters too. A ball of clay sinks, but the same clay pressed into a wide bowl can float. Boat builders use this trick: they spread the weight out over more water.
Always predict before you test! Scientists make a guess first (your hypothesis from Module 1), and then they check. Were you surprised by anything? A surprise is data, too.
lessons.try: Predict sink or float for 6 household objects, then test them in a tub. Which prediction surprised you most?

build.title: Ramp Racers
build.mission: Run a fair test: does ramp height change how far a car rolls?
materials: Paper and pencil for your data table
steps: Ask your QUESTION: does a higher ramp make the car roll farther? Write your HYPOTHESIS.
Set the ramp LOW (1 book). Release the car from the top — do not push. Measure how far it rolls past the ramp. Repeat 3 times.
Raise the ramp to MEDIUM (2 books). Repeat 3 runs. Then HIGH (3 books). Repeat 3 runs.
Record every run in a table. Find the average distance for each height.
Draw your CONCLUSION: did height matter? Was your hypothesis right?
think: Why do we release instead of push?
Why repeat each height 3 times?
What would happen with a heavier car? How could you test it fairly?
build.science: You controlled variables, repeated trials, and averaged results — the exact method professional engineers use when they test everything from car brakes to airplane wings.

mods.title: Measurement & Data
mods.intro: Numbers turn guesses into knowledge. In this module you will master rulers, walk perimeters, cover areas, fill volumes, and turn messy measurements into clean graphs that reveal the truth at a glance.
objs: Measure length accurately with a ruler.
Estimate before measuring.
Calculate perimeter, area, and volume.
Read and build bar graphs.

lessons.title: Rulers and Estimates
paras: A ruler turns "kind of long" into "exactly 7 inches." Line up the zero mark with one end of the object. Then read the number at the other end. Engineers say, "Measure twice, cut once," because checking is better than guessing.

Before you measure, ESTIMATE. An estimate is a smart guess, like "I think the book is 6 blocks long." Then measure and compare. Estimating trains your brain to sense size, and engineers do it all the time.
Pick the right unit for the job. Use inches or centimeters for small things, feet or meters for rooms, and miles or kilometers for long trips.
Using the wrong units can cause real disasters. A famous spacecraft was lost because one team used pounds (imperial units) and another team used newtons (metric units).
lessons.try: Estimate the length of your shoe in blocks, then measure it. How close was your estimate? Try again with your hand — are you getting better?

lessons.title: Perimeter and Area
paras: PERIMETER is the trip around a shape. Walk every edge and add the lengths. A rectangle 4 by 3 has perimeter 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 units. Fences, picture frames, and running tracks are all perimeter problems.

AREA is how much flat space a shape covers — count the unit squares inside. That same 4-by-3 rectangle covers 12 squares. Floors, carpets, and gardens are area problems: area tells builders how much material to buy.
Shortcut for rectangles: perimeter = 2 × (length + width), and area = length × width. But never trust a shortcut you can't explain — walk the edges and count the squares first, then use the fast way.
lessons.try: Find the perimeter and area of your bedroom door in footsteps. Then check: does area = length × width match your square count?

lessons.title: Volume: Filling Space
paras: VOLUME measures how much 3D space something fills, counted in cubes. A box that is 4 cubes long, 3 cubes wide, and 2 cubes tall holds 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cubes. Each layer holds 12 cubes, and there are 2 layers.
Volume answers the question "How much fits inside?" It tells you how much air fills a room, how much water fills a pool, or how many boxes fit in a moving truck.
Length × width × height works for boxes. For strange shapes, scientists drop the object in water and measure how much the water rises. The rise is equal to the object's volume. Clever!
lessons.try: How many sugar cubes (or dice) fit in a small box? Predict first, then fill it layer by layer. Multiply length × width × height — does it match?

lessons.title: Graphs Tell the Story
paras: A bar graph compares amounts so your eyes can see the winner instantly. Taller bar = bigger number. Scientists graph data because patterns hide in tables but jump out in pictures.
To build one: label what you measured along the bottom, mark numbers up the side, and draw one bar per item. Keep bar widths equal and leave gaps between bars.
Reading a graph is a superpower. Which bar is tallest? How much taller? Are any bars equal? Every news chart, sports stat, and science report is asking you these same questions.
lessons.try: Count the books in three rooms of your home. Make a bar graph of the results. Which room wins — and by how many books?

build.title: Measure Your World
build.mission: Estimate, measure, and graph five objects — then judge your estimating skill with data.
steps: Choose 5 objects. For each, ESTIMATE its length in inches and write it down. No measuring yet!
Now MEASURE each object carefully, lining up the zero mark. Record the real lengths.
For each object, find your error: how far off was your estimate?
Build a BAR GRAPH with two bars per object — estimate vs. real. Label everything.
Compute your average error. Set a goal: can you get your average error under 1 inch next time?
think: Which objects were hardest to estimate? Why?
Did your estimates get better as you went? What did your brain learn?
Where would bad estimating cause real problems?
build.science: You calibrated a mental instrument — your own sense of size. Carpenters, surgeons, and pilots all train this same skill: estimate first, verify with tools, track the error, improve.

mods.title: Geometry & Architecture
mods.intro: Buildings are geometry you can walk through. In this module you will see shapes hiding in skylines, mirror buildings in half, shrink rooms onto paper, measure angles like a pro, and read blueprints from a bird's-eye view.
objs: Identify shapes and angles in real structures.
Use symmetry to complete designs.
Draw to scale and read top-view blueprints.
Decode basic blueprint symbols.

lessons.title: Shapes in the Skyline
paras: Look at any city: triangle roofs, rectangle walls, circle windows, arch doorways. Architects compose buildings from shapes the way writers compose sentences from words.

Some shapes are structural heroes. The TRIANGLE is the strongest shape — it cannot wobble without changing its side lengths, which is why bridges wear triangle armor called trusses. ARCHES and DOMES are curve heroes: they spread weight along their curve instead of letting it pile in one spot.
Once you see shapes in buildings, you cannot unsee them. That is the beginning of architectural vision.
lessons.try: Shape hunt! Look at the nearest building and list every shape you can find. Can you spot a triangle doing structural work?

lessons.title: Symmetry: Nature's Favorite Trick
paras: SYMMETRY means one half mirrors the other. Draw an imaginary line down the middle of a butterfly: left matches right. Buildings love symmetry because it looks balanced and distributes weight evenly.
To test for symmetry, fold the shape along the suspected mirror line. If both halves match exactly, you found it. Some shapes have many mirror lines (a square has four); some have none.
Architects use symmetry as a shortcut: design half the building, mirror it, and the design is done. Nature invented the trick first — your face is (almost) symmetric.
lessons.try: Draw half a house on folded paper, then trace the mirror half. Open it — perfect symmetry! Now find 3 symmetric objects in your home.

lessons.title: Scale: Small Paper, Big Building
paras: Architects draw buildings small and build them big using SCALE. A scale like '1 square = 2 feet' is a promise: every square on paper stands for 2 feet of real building.
To use scale, divide real feet by feet-per-square. A 12-by-16-foot room at 1 square = 2 feet becomes 6 by 8 squares. Get the scale wrong and the door won't fit — a mistake that costs real money.
Scale models work the same way in 3D. A dollhouse is a house at tiny scale. Engineers test ideas on models before committing to the full-size build.
lessons.try: On graph paper, draw your bedroom at 1 square = 1 foot. Measure your real room first — does your drawing match?

lessons.title: Angles and Blueprints
paras: An ANGLE tells you how wide a corner opens. We measure angles in degrees. A square corner is called a RIGHT ANGLE, and it measures 90°. Buildings are full of right angles, like where walls meet floors and where window frames join.
A protractor is the tool that measures angles. Steep angles, like 45° braces, fight sideways pushes. Wide, low angles spread weight out. Every angle in a building has a job.

BLUEPRINTS are maps for builders, drawn as if you were looking down from above. They use symbols: thick lines for walls, double lines for windows, and a gap with a curved line for a door. Reading the symbols lets you "see" the building before it exists.
lessons.try: Angle hunt! Find and count every right angle in one room. Then sketch the room's top view — your first blueprint.

build.title: Dream Room Floor Plan
build.mission: Draft a real, to-scale floor plan of your dream bedroom — like a working architect.
steps: Set your scale: 1 square = 1 foot. Measure your real bedroom's length and width.
Draw the room's walls on graph paper at scale. Double-check your math.
Add a DOOR (gap with swing arc) and at least one WINDOW (double lines in the wall).
Place furniture as labeled rectangles, drawn to scale. Can the door swing freely? Check your flow!
Present your plan: walk a partner through it like an architect pitching a client.
think: Does your door hit any furniture when it swings?
Which wall should hold the window for the best light?
What would you change if the room were 2 feet wider?
build.science: You just did schematic design — the first phase of real architecture. Every building on Earth started as lines on paper exactly like yours.

mods.title: Structures & Engineering
mods.intro: Measuring is done. Now the engineer's question: WILL IT HOLD? In this module you will build with triangles, balance loads, raise columns, stretch spans, and learn the golden loop of engineering — test, fail, fix, fly.
objs: Explain why triangles and trusses are strong.
Distinguish dead loads from live loads.
Describe how columns, beams, and span work together.
Apply the test-and-redesign loop to a real build.

lessons.title: Triangles and Trusses
paras: The triangle is the only shape that cannot wobble without stretching its sides. Push a square and it collapses into a diamond; push a triangle and it holds. That rigidity is why engineers build with them.

A TRUSS is a team of triangles joined into a framework. When weight presses down on one point, the triangles pass the force along to their neighbors until it reaches the ground. Load shared is load survived.
Look for trusses on real bridges, crane arms, and roof frames. Once you know the triangle trick, you will see it holding up the modern world.
lessons.try: Build a square from straws and tape, then a triangle. Push each sideways. Which wobbles? Now brace your square with a diagonal straw — what did you just build?

lessons.title: Loads: The Weight of the World
paras: Every structure carries two kinds of weight. DEAD LOAD is the building's own weight — steel, concrete, glass, always there. LIVE LOAD is everything temporary: people, furniture, cars, wind, snow.
Engineers add them up and then build stronger than the total, with a safety margin. A bridge rated for 10 tons is actually built to hold much more — because real life is full of surprises.
Too much load in the wrong place causes failure. That is why engineers test with weights before opening day, and why you will load-test your own bridge in this module's simulation.
lessons.try: List the dead loads and live loads on your kitchen table. Which live load would be the hardest to predict?

lessons.title: Columns, Beams, and Span
paras: COLUMNS stand and carry weight DOWN to the ground. BEAMS lie across and carry weight SIDEWAYS to the columns. Together they form the skeleton of almost every building.
Remove one column and the beam above must span farther — and longer spans are harder. SPAN is the distance between supports: short spans are easy, long spans demand deeper trusses and stronger beams.
This is why the longest bridges on Earth — suspension and cable-stayed giants — look so dramatic. Their spans are enormous, so their engineering must be extraordinary.
lessons.try: Lay a ruler between two books (a beam on columns). Press the middle — how much does it sag? Now stack two rulers. What changed, and why?

lessons.title: Test, Fail, Fix, Fly
paras: Here is the engineer's golden loop: TEST your design, let it FAIL, find the weak spot, FIX it, and test again. Every great bridge was once a broken model.

Failure is data. When a model falls down, it shows you exactly where the design was weakest. You could never learn that just by thinking. Engineers celebrate failures in the lab so they never happen in real life.

When you redesign, change only ONE thing at a time, just like a fair test from Module 1. Change the truss, then test again. Change the material, then test again. Small changes and honest notes lead to steady progress.
lessons.try: Build any tower from blocks. Load it until it falls. Before rebuilding, write down exactly where it failed — then fix only that spot.

lessons.title: Budgets: Engineering with Money
paras: Real projects have budgets — and the cheapest design that works usually wins. If a tile costs $2 and you need 12, that's 12 × $2 = $24. Add every material the same way.
CONSTRAINTS are rules your design must obey: budget caps, lot sizes, minimum rooms. Constraints aren't cages; they're the game. The best engineers win inside the rules.
Try it: 12 tiles at $2 ($24), 4 beams at $5 ($20), 2 windows at $8 ($16). Total: $60. Now ask — could you redesign to hit $50 without breaking the rules?
lessons.try: Price a dream treehouse. List 5 materials with a price and an amount for each. What is your total? Now cut your total by 20%. What would you change?

build.title: The Paper Bridge Challenge
build.mission: Engineer a paper bridge that holds the most pennies — then redesign it to hold more.
steps: Set the books 4 inches apart. Lay a flat sheet across — your first beam bridge.
PREDICT how many pennies it will hold. Then load pennies in the center, one at a time, until it collapses. Record the number.
REDESIGN: fold a new sheet into an accordion (W-shape) or add triangle trusses. Predict again.
Test your redesign the same fair way. Record the new number.
Compare: which design won, and by how much? Write your conclusion like an engineer.
think: Where did the flat bridge fail first — middle or ends?
Why does folding make paper stronger without adding weight?
What would you try on a third design?
build.science: Folding puts more material farther from the center, which resists bending — the same reason steel beams are shaped like the letter I. You just discovered structural engineering's favorite trick.

mods.title: Energy & Circuits
mods.intro: ENERGY is the ability to do work. Energy never disappears. It only changes from one form to another. In this module you will follow energy from batteries to bulbs, build real circuits, and learn why a broken loop means darkness.
objs: Define energy and name its forms.
Trace energy transfers in everyday devices.
Build a working circuit with a switch.
Explain what happens when a circuit breaks.

lessons.title: What Is Energy?
paras: ENERGY is the ability to do work — to move something, heat something, or light something up. A rolling ball has motion energy. A hot stove has heat energy. A flashlight beam is light energy.
Energy never disappears; it TRANSFERS from one form to another. Rub your hands fast: motion energy becomes heat energy. A toaster turns electrical energy into heat and light.
Everything you do runs on energy transfers. Eating transfers food energy into motion energy. A car transfers gasoline energy into motion (and a lot of heat).
lessons.try: Energy hunt! Find 5 energy transfers happening in your home right now. For each, name the starting form and the ending form.

lessons.title: Circuits: The Electric Loop
paras: A CIRCUIT is a closed loop that electricity flows around: battery → wire → bulb → wire → back to the battery. If the loop breaks anywhere, the flow stops and the bulb goes dark.

Each part has a job. The BATTERY is the pump that pushes electricity around the loop. The WIRES are the pipes, and they must be made of conductors like copper or aluminum. The BULB is where electrical energy turns into light and heat.
Electricity needs a complete path. One loose wire, one gap, or one break, and nothing works. Electricians spend a lot of their time hunting for breaks in loops.
lessons.try: Draw a circuit with a battery, two wires, and a bulb. Now draw the same circuit with one wire disconnected. Label what happens.

lessons.title: Switches and Control
paras: A SWITCH is a deliberate break in the circuit that you can open and close. Flip it closed: the loop completes and the bulb lights. Flip it open: the loop breaks and darkness returns.
Every light switch, power button, and remote control is just a fancy circuit-breaker. Engineers design switches to be safe, quick, and reliable — a switch that sparks or sticks is a failed design.
Advanced circuits add more parts in the loop: buzzers, motors, sensors. But the rule never changes — no closed loop, no flow.
lessons.try: Find 5 switches in your home. For each, figure out what circuit it opens and closes. Bonus: find one switch that controls something surprising.

build.title: Light It Up: The Paper Circuit Card
build.mission: Build a real working circuit on a greeting card — with a switch you design yourself.
steps: SAFETY: a grown-up must handle the coin battery. Never put it in your mouth, and keep coin batteries away from little kids and pets. Swallowing one is an emergency — call 911 right away.
Plan your loop on paper: battery → copper tape path → LED legs → copper tape path → battery. The LED's longer leg connects toward the battery's + side.
Lay copper tape along your planned path on the card. Press the LED legs onto the tape and tape them down.
Slide the battery under the tape at the gap — does the LED light? If not, debug: check every connection (Module 7 skills!).
Add your SWITCH: leave a gap in one tape path and bridge it with a paperclip. Clip on = light. Clip off = dark. Decorate your card!
think: Which LED leg had to touch which battery side?
What happened when you flipped the battery over?
Where exactly did you put the switch, and why does that spot work?
build.science: You built a series circuit — the same basic loop inside flashlights and toys. Engineers prototype electronics on paper and breadboards before manufacturing anything.

mods.title: Code & Logic
mods.intro: Code is just instructions written precisely enough for a machine to follow. In this module you will write algorithms, read flowcharts, hunt bugs, count in binary, and crack secret ciphers — the same ideas behind every app you love.
objs: Write clear step-by-step algorithms.
Read and follow flowcharts.
Debug broken instructions.
Count in binary and decode a Caesar cipher.

lessons.title: Algorithms: Recipes for Everything
paras: An ALGORITHM is step-by-step instructions that solve a problem: a recipe, a morning routine, directions to a friend's house. Computers follow algorithms written as code.

Good algorithms are PRECISE. 'Go to the store' is vague; 'walk 2 blocks north, turn right, enter the store with the red sign' is an algorithm. Machines do exactly what you say — so you must say exactly what you mean.
You already think algorithmically when you give directions or teach a game. Programming just writes that thinking down so a machine can run it.
lessons.try: Write an algorithm for making a sandwich with at least 8 steps. Have someone follow it EXACTLY as written — no common sense allowed! What broke?

lessons.title: Flowcharts and Debugging
paras: A FLOWCHART draws an algorithm as shapes: ovals for start/stop, rectangles for steps, diamonds for decisions. Following the arrows shows the exact path of the program.
A BUG is a mistake in the instructions. Maybe a step is missing, in the wrong order, or unclear. DEBUGGING means hunting the bug: test each step, find where reality differs from the plan, and fix it.
Professional programmers spend more time debugging than writing. Finding bugs isn't failure — it's the job. The best debuggers are patient, systematic, and a little bit stubborn.
lessons.try: Draw a flowchart for 'getting ready for school' with one decision diamond (e.g., 'Is it raining?'). Trade with a partner and follow theirs exactly.

lessons.title: Binary: Counting with Two Digits
paras: Computers count with only 0 and 1 — BINARY. Each position is worth double the last: 1, 2, 4, 8... To read binary, add the values where you see 1s. So 101 means 4 + 0 + 1 = 5.
Why only two digits? Because computer switches are either ON (1) or OFF (0). Everything digital — photos, music, games — is ultimately long strings of 1s and 0s.
Practice: 11 in binary = 2 + 1 = 3. 100 = 4. 110 = 4 + 2 = 6. You are now reading the native language of machines.
lessons.try: Convert these to regular numbers: 10, 101, 111. Then write YOUR age in binary.

lessons.title: Ciphers: Secret Codes
paras: A CIPHER is a secret code that scrambles a message so only people with the key can read it. The Caesar cipher moves every letter forward by the same number. With a shift of 3, A becomes D, B becomes E, and HELLO becomes KHOOR.
To decode a message, shift each letter backward by the same number. KHOOR with a shift of 3 becomes HELLO again. The shift number is called the KEY. Without the key, the message is hard to read.
Real internet security uses the same idea with much bigger keys. When you see a little padlock in a web browser, ciphers are protecting your information.
lessons.try: Encode your name with a Caesar shift of 3. Trade with a partner and decode each other's. Now try shift 5 — is it harder?

build.title: The Human Robot Maze
build.mission: Program a human 'robot' through a maze using only precise algorithms — then debug it.
steps: Build a simple maze on the floor with tape. Mark a START and a FINISH.
The programmer writes an ALGORITHM using only these commands: STEP FORWARD, TURN LEFT, TURN RIGHT.
The 'robot' (partner) follows the algorithm EXACTLY — no fixing mistakes mid-run, no common sense.
When the robot crashes or gets lost, DEBUG together: which step was the bug? Fix it and re-run.
Swap roles. Then add a rule: the algorithm must use a LOOP (e.g., 'repeat 3 times: step forward').
think: Which bugs were hardest to find?
How did writing it down change the way you thought?
Where did you need a loop, and what did it replace?
build.science: You just did pair programming: one writes, one runs, both debug. Real software teams work exactly this way — and every robot on Mars runs algorithms debugged by humans first.

mods.title: The Living Lab
mods.intro: The most amazing machine you will ever study is yourself. In this module you will map your body's systems, decode food as fuel, learn how your brain handles stress, and use real math to measure your own health.
objs: Describe how the heart, lungs, and brain work together.
Sort foods by how they fuel the body.
Use breathing and habits to manage stress and sleep.
Measure pulse and hydration with math.

lessons.title: Your Body's Systems
paras: Your HEART is a muscle pump that beats about 100,000 times a day, pushing blood to every cell. Your LUNGS trade air: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out. Your BRAIN is mission control, running everything — including itself.
Systems teamwork: run fast and your muscles need more oxygen, so your heart beats faster and your lungs breathe harder. Your brain coordinates the whole response without you thinking about it.
Like any machine, your body needs the right fuel, regular rest, and maintenance. That maintenance has a name: health.
lessons.try: Find your pulse in your wrist. Count beats for 15 seconds, then multiply by 4. That's your resting heart rate — write it down for the Pulse Lab!

lessons.title: Food Is Fuel
paras: Food is fuel and building material. PROTEINS build muscles, CARBOHYDRATES give quick energy, and FRUITS AND VEGETABLES deliver vitamins that keep systems running. Water carries it all.
SUGAR is fuel too — but the fast, crashy kind. A soda floods your body with sugar all at once; an apple delivers sugar slowly with fiber. Same sweetness, very different ride.
Rainbow rule: the more colors on your plate from plants, the more nutrients you're getting. Engineers would call this diversifying your fuel supply.
lessons.try: Sugar detective! Check two drink labels (or look them up). How many grams of sugar in each? Which would you choose — and why?

lessons.title: Your Brain on Stress
paras: STRESS is your body's alarm: heart pounds, breathing quickens, muscles tense. It evolved to help you escape danger — useful for tigers, less useful for math tests.
You can hack the alarm with your breath. Slow breathing tells your brain 'we're safe,' and the alarm quiets. Try it: breathe in 4 counts, hold 4, out 4, hold 4. That's square breathing.

SLEEP is the brain's nightly reset — it files memories and repairs the body. HABITS are actions your brain runs on autopilot; build good ones (like a bedtime routine) and they work for you automatically.
lessons.try: Do 2 minutes of square breathing. Rate your stress 1–10 before and after. What changed? Write it down — that's data!

lessons.title: Health Math
paras: Your body runs on numbers. PULSE: count beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 to get beats per minute. Compare resting vs. active — the difference shows your heart responding to demand.
HYDRATION math: if your goal is 8 cups of water and you've had 3, you need 5 more. Simple subtraction keeps your body's systems running smoothly.
Track it like a scientist: measure daily, graph weekly, look for patterns. Athletes, doctors, and astronauts all run their bodies on data.
lessons.try: Track your water cups for 3 days. Graph the results as a bar chart. Did you hit 8 cups? What pattern do you see?

build.title: The Pulse Lab
build.mission: Measure how exercise changes your heart rate — and prove it with a graph.
steps: Sit quietly for 2 minutes. Find your wrist pulse. Count beats for 15 seconds, multiply by 4. Record your RESTING rate.
Do jumping jacks for 1 minute. IMMEDIATELY count for 15 seconds, multiply by 4. Record your ACTIVE rate.
Rest 2 minutes. Measure again. Record your RECOVERY rate.
Find the differences: active minus resting, active minus recovery.
Draw a BAR GRAPH with 3 bars: resting, active, recovery. Label everything. Write your conclusion.
think: How much higher was your active rate?
How fast did your pulse recover? What does fast recovery suggest?
Why multiply the 15-second count by 4 instead of counting for a full minute?
build.science: You measured cardiac response — the same test doctors use to check heart fitness. Athletes track exactly these numbers to train smarter.

intro.welcome: This guide is for the grown-up leading the course: a homeschool parent, classroom teacher, tutor, or after-school leader. You do not need a science background. Every lesson already tells students what to do. Your job is to set up materials, keep everyone safe, ask good questions, and notice what each child understands.
formats: One module per week. Two sessions of 45 to 60 minutes each: lessons and labs in the first session, build project and quiz in the second.
One module every one to two weeks. Teach lessons as a group, run labs in pairs, and run build projects in teams of three or four with assigned roles.
Sixteen sessions of about 60 minutes. Each module takes two sessions. Start every session with a 5-minute warm-up question from the last lesson.
session: Ask one question from the last lesson. Let two or three students answer in their own words.
Read or listen to the lesson and watch its video. Pause after each paragraph and ask, "What does that mean in your own words?"
Do the lesson's TRY IT activity. Walk around and listen more than you talk.
Run the module's interactive lab, or the hands-on build project on the second day.
Each student says one thing they learned and one question they still have. Write the questions down for next time.
ages: Read lessons aloud together. Use the Listen button and the videos. Accept spoken answers on quizzes and write them down for the child. Do the build projects side by side.
Students read on their own and talk through answers with a partner. Expect written data tables in build projects.
Students lead. Ask them to explain the science to a younger learner, and to design their own fair test as an extension.

safety: Never taste or touch unknown materials. In Module 1, powders are for looking at, touching only when you allow it, and mixing with water. They are never for tasting.
Coin batteries (Module 6) must be handled by a grown-up. Keep them away from young children and pets. Swallowing one is a medical emergency: call 911 right away.
Supervise anything with water, ramps on tables, or stacks of books so nothing falls on feet or hands.
In the Pulse Lab (Module 8), students only exercise if they feel well. Stop at once if a child feels dizzy, short of breath, or has chest pain. The Pulse Lab is for learning, not medical advice.
Keep cords, outlets, and household electricity out of every activity. All circuit work uses one small coin battery only.
Clean up spills right away, and wash hands after the powder lab and after handling pennies.

assess.overview: Grade two kinds of work: the quizzes (right or wrong) and the build projects (graded with a rubric). Quizzes check that students remember the ideas. Build projects check that students can use them.
scoring: 8 questions each, 1 point per question, 64 points total. A score of 6 or more is a pass.
24 questions, 1 point each. A score of 22 or more (90%) earns the STEM Master title, certificate, and badge.
Scored with the 4-level rubric in each module. Use it for feedback, not for a pass or fail.
levels: Needs a lot of help. Can name the idea but cannot use it yet.
Can use the idea with some help or reminders. Some steps or records are missing.
Uses the idea correctly on their own. Records are complete and the conclusion matches the data.
Uses the idea correctly, explains why it works, and improves or extends the test on their own.
assess.retake: Students may retake any module quiz as many times as they like. The course keeps their best score. Before a retake, have the student restudy the lessons tied to the questions they missed (see the Answer Key). For the final exam, allow a retake after one more day of review.
assess.badge: Award the STEM Master certificate and badge when a student scores 22 or more out of 24 on the final exam. In the interactive course, the student types their name on the certificate page to print the certificate and download their badge.

finalAdmin: Review: the day before, have students retake any module quiz they scored below 7 on.
Setting: give the exam in one sitting of about 30 to 40 minutes. Read questions aloud to younger learners if needed.
Grading: use the Final Exam Answers in the Answer Key. Accept any answer that matches the meaning of the key, even if worded differently.
STEM Master: 22 or more correct out of 24 earns the title, the certificate, and the badge.
Not there yet: if a student scores below 22, review the lessons tied to the missed questions and allow a retake on another day.

1.big: Scientists learn by observing carefully, sorting, finding patterns, and running fair tests.
time: Session 1
Lessons 1.1 to 1.4 with videos, TRY IT activities, and the Pattern Lab
Session 2
Build: The Mystery Powder Lab, then the Module 1 quiz
prep: Salt, sugar, and baking soda in three cups labeled A, B and C (grown-up labels them)
3 spoons, a magnifier, and 3 cups of water
20 small objects for sorting (buttons, coins, blocks)
Two ice cubes for the Lesson 1.4 TRY IT
coach: 1.1 Five Super-Senses
Ask for observations, not opinions. If a child says "It's pretty," ask, "What do you see that makes it look pretty?"
1.2 Sorting
Have students name their sorting rule out loud before they sort, then re-sort by a new rule.
1.3 Patterns
Ask, "What's the rule?" before "What's next?" The rule is the science.
1.4 Scientific Method
Celebrate a wrong hypothesis. Say, "Great, now we know something true!"
mis: "An opinion is an observation."
Sort sentences into two piles: what anyone could check, and what someone feels.
"A fair test can change two things."
Run the ramp or ice test changing two things at once, then ask, "Which change caused it?"
1.support: Give sentence starters such as "I see...", "It feels..." and "I think... because...".
1.stretch: Add a fourth mystery powder (cornstarch or flour) and have students design a new test to tell it apart.
prompts: How did you know which powder was which? What was your evidence?
Why should scientists never taste unknown things?
rubric: Lists one or two vague details
Lists color or texture for each powder
Records color, grain size, feel, and water result for all three
Adds measured or compared details, such as which dissolved fastest
Clear table with a note on what surprised them
Names the powders with weak evidence
Names each powder with evidence from the table
Explains which test was most useful and why

2.big: Forces are pushes and pulls. Friction, gravity, magnets, and density change how things move, float, and sink.
time: Session 1
Lessons 2.1 to 2.4 with videos, TRY IT activities, and the Ramp Racer Simulator
Session 2
Build: Ramp Racers, then the Module 2 quiz
prep: A board or tray for a ramp, and books to raise it
A toy car, and a ruler or measuring tape
A magnet, paperclips, and string
A tub of water and 6 small household objects for sink or float
coach: 2.1 Pushes and Pulls
Have students act out a push and a pull, then name the direction of each.
2.2 Friction and Ramps
Ask what stays the same in a fair ramp test before anyone races.
2.3 Magnets
Let students predict which objects a magnet will pull before testing. Many expect all metals to stick.
2.4 Sink or Float
Always predict first. Record every prediction, even wrong ones.
mis: "Heavy things always sink."
Float a large orange, then peel it and try again. Talk about the air in the peel.
"Magnets attract all metals."
Test a coin, foil, and a paperclip. Only iron and steel stick.
2.support: Mark the release line on the ramp with tape so the fair-test rule is easy to follow.
2.stretch: Test a fourth ramp height, or change the surface instead, and graph the results.
prompts: Why do we let go of the car instead of pushing it?
Why run each height three times?
rubric: Explains why each other thing stayed the same
Measured all 9 runs from the same point
Measured carefully and noticed odd results
Uses averages to explain the trend
States if the hypothesis was supported, using data
Suggests the next test to run

3.big: Measuring turns guesses into facts. Perimeter goes around, area covers, volume fills, and graphs show the story.
time: Session 1
Lessons 3.1 to 3.4 with videos, TRY IT activities, and the Measure Lab
Session 2
Build: Measure Your World, then the Module 3 quiz
prep: Rulers and a measuring tape
5 objects of different sizes
Graph paper and crayons
Sugar cubes or dice and a small box for the volume TRY IT
coach: 3.1 Rulers and Estimates
Check that every ruler starts at zero, not at the edge of the ruler.
3.2 Perimeter and Area
Have students walk the edge for perimeter and count the squares for area before using a formula.
3.3 Volume
Build the box layer by layer so students see why we multiply three numbers.
3.4 Graphs
Ask, "Which bar is tallest? By how much?" for every graph.
mis: "Perimeter and area are the same thing."
Use the same rectangle: walk around it (perimeter), then fill it with squares (area).
"Start measuring at the end of the ruler."
Show the gap before the zero mark on most rulers and measure again.
3.support: Use a large grid on the floor with tape so students can step out perimeter and count area squares.
3.stretch: Find two rectangles with the same area but different perimeters.
prompts: Where would a bad estimate cause a real problem?
Did your estimates get better? Why?
rubric: Estimate for every object before measuring
Estimates improve and the student explains how
Inaccurate, starts at the ruler edge
Accurate, starts at zero, correct units
Accurate and checks with a second measurement
Labeled bar graph with estimate and real bars
Clear graph that shows the average error
Explains which objects were hard and why
Sets and explains a goal to improve

4.big: Buildings are made of shapes, symmetry, scale, and angles, and blueprints show them from above.
time: Session 1
Lessons 4.1 to 4.4 with videos, TRY IT activities, and the Angle Spotter
Session 2
Build: Dream Room Floor Plan, then the Module 4 quiz
prep: Graph paper, rulers, pencils and erasers
A measuring tape for the bedroom
Paper for folding symmetry shapes
coach: 4.1 Shapes in the Skyline
Take a short shape walk, or look at a photo of a building, and list every shape.
4.2 Symmetry
Fold, then check. If the halves do not match, it is not a line of symmetry.
4.3 Scale
Write the scale at the top of every page: 1 square = 1 foot.
4.4 Angles and Blueprints
Use the corner of a sheet of paper as a 90-degree angle checker.
mis: "A bigger drawing means a bigger room."
Show the same room drawn at two scales and compare the real sizes.
"Angles depend on how long the lines are."
Draw the same angle with short and long arms. The opening is the same.
4.support: Give students a pre-drawn room outline at scale, so they focus on the door, window, and furniture.
4.stretch: Design a second floor plan with a budget, using Lesson 5.5 prices.
prompts: Does your door hit any furniture when it swings?
What would you change if the room were 2 feet wider?
rubric: Every wall drawn correctly to scale
Furniture is also exactly to scale
Correct wall, door, and window symbols
Adds a legend that explains each symbol
Door swings freely and everything fits
Explains choices for light and flow
Walked a partner through the plan

5.big: Engineers build strong structures with triangles, plan for loads, and improve designs by testing and fixing.
time: Session 1
Lessons 5.1 to 5.5 with videos, TRY IT activities, and the Bridge Load Lab
Session 2
Build: The Paper Bridge Challenge, then the Module 5 quiz
prep: Paper sheets and tape
Two books of the same height
50 or more pennies or washers
Straws for the Lesson 5.1 TRY IT
coach: 5.1 Triangles and Trusses
Let students feel a square of straws wobble before they add the diagonal.
5.2 Loads
Sort loads in the room into dead loads (always there) and live loads (they come and go).
5.3 Columns, Beams, and Span
Press a ruler between two books, then move the books farther apart.
5.4 Test, Fail, Fix, Fly
Praise good failure records: where it broke, and why.
5.5 Budgets
Have students check each other's totals with a calculator.
mis: "Stronger means more material."
Compare a flat sheet and a folded sheet of the same paper.
"Failure means you did it wrong."
Show that every redesign starts from a failure record.
5.support: Give students the folding pattern for the accordion bridge so they can focus on testing.
5.stretch: Set a budget of paper and tape, and challenge teams to hold the most pennies per sheet.
prompts: Where did the flat bridge fail first, the middle or the ends?
Why does folding make paper stronger without adding weight?
rubric: Same supports and center loading every time
Redesign aimed at the weak spot
Redesign explained with trusses or folding
Explains the science of why it won

6.big: Energy changes form but never disappears. A closed circuit lets electricity flow, and a switch controls it.
time: Session 1
Lessons 6.1 to 6.3 with videos, TRY IT activities, and the Circuit Lab
Session 2
Build: Light It Up, The Paper Circuit Card, then the Module 6 quiz
prep: CR2032 coin batteries (grown-up keeps and hands out)
Copper tape or foil strips, small LEDs, and tape
Index cards or cardstock, and paperclips
coach: 6.1 What Is Energy?
Have students rub their hands fast and name the change: motion into heat.
6.2 Circuits
Trace the loop with a finger: battery, wire, bulb, wire, back to the battery.
6.3 Switches
Point to a light switch and ask, "Where is the gap in this loop?"
mis: "Electricity gets used up in the bulb."
Electricity flows around the loop. The bulb changes electrical energy into light and heat.
"One wire is enough."
Try lighting an LED with one connection, then two. It needs a complete loop.
6.support: Pre-draw the copper tape path on the card so students only lay the tape and place the LED.
6.stretch: Add a second LED and compare the brightness when the LEDs are side by side or in a line.
prompts: Which LED leg had to touch which battery side?
What happened when you flipped the battery over?
6.build: Light It Up: The Paper Circuit Card
rubric: Lights on its own and stays lit
Lights reliably and the student explains the loop
Switch opens and closes the loop every time
Explains why the switch works in that spot
Found and fixed a problem on their own
Explained the bug and how they found it

7.big: Code is precise instructions. Programmers use algorithms, flowcharts, debugging, binary, and ciphers.
time: Session 1
Lessons 7.1 to 7.4 with videos, TRY IT activities, and the Code Lab
Session 2
Build: The Human Robot Maze, then the Module 7 quiz
prep: Painter's tape or chalk for a floor maze
Paper, pencils, and command cards (FORWARD, LEFT, RIGHT)
A blindfold (optional)
coach: 7.1 Algorithms
Follow a student's sandwich algorithm exactly, word for word. The funny mistakes teach precision.
7.2 Flowcharts and Debugging
Ask, "Which step was the bug?" instead of "What went wrong?"
7.3 Binary
Use four cards worth 8, 4, 2 and 1. Flip them face up for 1 and face down for 0.
7.4 Ciphers
Make a letter wheel or strip so students can shift letters without counting on fingers.
mis: "The computer knows what I mean."
Run the human robot: it only does exactly what is written.
"Binary 10 means ten."
Use the place-value cards: 10 in binary is one 2 and no 1s, so it equals 2.
7.support: Start the maze with only FORWARD and one turn, then add more turns.
7.stretch: Add a LOOP command (repeat 3 times) and rewrite the program in fewer lines.
prompts: Which bugs were hardest to find?
Where did you need a loop, and what did it replace?
rubric: Precise steps that reach the finish
Explains each bug and its fix
Uses loops to shorten the program a lot
Coached a partner through a bug

8.big: Your body is a system. Food, breathing, sleep, and habits keep it running, and health math helps you track it.
time: Session 1
Lessons 8.1 to 8.4 with videos, TRY IT activities, and the Pulse Lab
Session 2
Build: The Pulse Lab, then the Module 8 quiz and final exam review
prep: A watch or timer with seconds
Paper, pencils, and crayons
Open space for jumping jacks
Two drink labels for the sugar TRY IT
coach: 8.1 Body Systems
Have students place a hand on their chest after jumping and feel the heart speed up.
8.2 Food Is Fuel
Talk about food without calling foods good or bad. Focus on fast and slow fuel.
8.3 Your Brain on Stress
Practice square breathing together at the start of the session.
8.4 Health Math
Model the 15 seconds times 4 math on the board before students try it.
mis: "Stress is always bad."
Stress is an alarm that helps in danger. We learn to turn it down when it is not needed.
"Count the full minute or it won't work."
Count 15 seconds and multiply by 4. The answer is close to a full-minute count.
8.support: Count the pulse together out loud, and let students use a calculator to multiply by 4.
8.stretch: Graph pulse recovery every 30 seconds for 2 minutes and describe the pattern.
prompts: How much higher was your active rate?
rubric: Counted resting, active and recovery rates
Correct times-4 math for all three
States the active rate was higher

how: A Family STEM Night is one 45-minute evening per module. Kids lead, grown-ups help, and everybody does the science together.
It works at a kitchen table, in a classroom, at a library, or at a church or community center. For a group, set up one table per family.
Before the night, watch that module's videos together in the course (about 10 minutes). Mia, Malik and Nana introduce the ideas you will use.
Give everyone a job. Jobs rotate each night so every person gets a turn.
roles: reads the steps out loud and keeps the team on track
writes down predictions and results in the data box
watches the clock for each part of the night
handles the materials and sets up each test

nights.title: Mystery Bag Detectives
nights.big: Scientists observe carefully and sort by rules.
materials: 8 to 12 safe household objects (a spoon, a sock, a pinecone, a block, a cotton ball, a key)
nights.warm: Clap a pattern (clap, clap, snap). The next person repeats it and adds one more beat. How long can the pattern grow before someone breaks it?
steps: A grown-up secretly puts 2 or 3 objects into each bag.
Each detective reaches in without looking and describes one object using only touch: rough or smooth, heavy or light, warm or cool, hard or soft.
The Recorder writes each description. Then everyone guesses what the object is.
Dump the bags out. Check your guesses.
Now sort all the objects using a rule your family invents, like 'things that bend' or 'things made of metal.' Sort them again with a different rule.
talk: Which description helped most with guessing? Why?
What was an observation, and what was an opinion?
How many different sorting rules did your family find?
nights.safety: Use only objects a grown-up has checked. No sharp, hot, or breakable things in the bags. Nothing goes in anyone's mouth.

nights.title: Cardboard Mini-Golf
nights.big: Forces start, stop, and change how things move.
materials: Cardboard, a book, or a tray for ramps
A towel, aluminum foil, and wax paper
A cup on its side for the hole
nights.warm: Push-or-pull charades: one person acts out an everyday motion (opening a door, kicking a ball). Everyone shouts PUSH or PULL.
steps: Lay the cup on its side on the floor. That is the hole.
Build a ramp and tape down walls to make a mini-golf course.
Roll the ball down the ramp. Count how many tries it takes to reach the hole.
Cover the floor path with the towel, then foil, then wax paper. Roll from the same spot each time.
The Recorder notes which surface let the ball roll farthest. Which one had the most friction?
talk: Which surface was the 'grabbiest'? How did you know?
What changed when the ramp was taller?
Where do you see friction help people every day?
nights.safety: Keep the course on the floor and away from stairs. Roll balls gently and watch for small children and pets.

nights.title: The Family Measure-Off
nights.big: Measuring and graphing turn guesses into evidence.
materials: Paper and crayons for a bar graph
nights.warm: Estimation Station: everyone guesses how many steps it takes to cross the room. Then walk it and count. Whose guess was closest?
steps: PREDICT: is a person's arm span (fingertip to fingertip) about the same as their height?
Measure each family member's height (stand against a wall) and arm span. Use inches.
The Recorder writes both numbers on a sticky note for each person.
Make a bar graph: two bars for each person, one for height and one for arm span.
Look at the graph. Were the two bars close for most people?
talk: What did the graph show that the numbers alone did not?
Why do we measure from zero on the tape?
What else could your family measure and graph?
nights.safety: Measure standing on a flat floor. No climbing on furniture to reach.

nights.title: Shape Hunt and Mirror Art
nights.big: Shapes, symmetry, and angles are hiding everywhere.
nights.warm: I Spy Shapes: 'I spy a rectangle... a circle... a right angle.' Find each one in the room.
steps: Shape Hunt: in 5 minutes, list every triangle, circle, rectangle, and right angle you can find at home.
Fold a sheet of paper in half. Draw half of a butterfly, a face, or a building along the fold.
With a grown-up's help, cut along your line and unfold it. You made a symmetric shape. The fold is the mirror line.
Optional: stand a mirror on the fold of a half-drawing and watch the whole picture appear.
Hang your mirror art up and give your gallery a name.
talk: Which shape did your family find most? Why do builders use it so much?
Is your face perfectly symmetric? How could you check?
Where did you see right angles?
nights.safety: Grown-ups help with scissors. Use child-safe scissors if you have them.

nights.title: Newspaper Tower Showdown
nights.big: Engineers test, fail, fix, and test again.
materials: 10 sheets of newspaper or scrap paper per team
1 arm's length of masking tape per team
nights.warm: Triangle or square? Make each shape from 3 or 4 straws or rolled papers and tape. Press on a corner. Which one holds its shape?
steps: Goal: build the tallest tower that stands on its own and holds the paperback on top for 10 seconds.
Plan for 3 minutes. Draw your design before building.
Build for 12 minutes. Rolled tubes and triangles are strong ideas.
Test: set the book on top and count to 10. Measure the height.
Redesign for 5 minutes and test again. Did your changes help?
talk: What failed first, and what did that teach you?
Where did you use triangles?
If you had 5 more sheets, what would you change?
nights.safety: Build on the floor or a sturdy table. Keep the tower away from faces when testing.

nights.title: Static Electricity Show
nights.big: Energy can move, jump, and change form.
materials: Small bits of torn tissue paper
nights.warm: Energy freeze-tag: the caller names a kind of energy (light, sound, heat, motion). Everyone acts it out, then freezes.
steps: Blow up the balloon and tie it (a grown-up helps).
Rub the balloon on dry hair or a wool sweater for 10 seconds.
Hold it just above the tissue bits. What happens?
Turn the faucet on to a very thin, slow stream. Rub the comb on your hair and bring it close to the water without touching. Watch the water bend.
Try sticking the rubbed balloon to a wall. Time how long it stays.
talk: What did rubbing do to the balloon?
Where have you felt a little static shock before?
How is static different from the electricity in a circuit?
nights.safety: Balloons are a choking hazard for small children. Grown-ups handle the balloon and pick up broken pieces right away. Keep electronics away from the faucet.

nights.title: Robot Grown-Up and Binary Bracelets
nights.big: Computers follow exact steps, and they count in 0s and 1s.
materials: Paper cups or plastic cups (6 to 10)
Beads or paper squares in two colors
nights.warm: Simon Says, robot style: the 'robot' only moves when the command is exact. 'Raise your hand' gets a question back: 'Which hand? How high?'
steps: Kids write an algorithm (numbered steps) to stack cups into a pyramid.
A grown-up plays the robot and follows the steps EXACTLY as written, even if they are silly.
When the robot goes wrong, that is a bug. Debug the steps and run them again.
Binary bracelets: pick one color for 0 and one for 1. Use the code chart to spell your first initial.
Code chart (5 beads per letter): A 00001, B 00010, C 00011, D 00100, E 00101. Keep counting up in binary for the rest of the alphabet.
talk: What was the funniest bug? How did you fix it?
Why do computers need such exact steps?
Can someone read your bracelet without the chart?
nights.safety: Beads are a choking hazard for children under 3. Store them away when you finish.

nights.title: Reaction Lab and Calm-Down Breathing
nights.big: Your body runs on numbers, and you can measure it.
nights.warm: Square breathing together: breathe in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4. Do it three times.
steps: Reaction test: a partner holds the ruler at the top. You hold your thumb and finger open at the 0 mark, not touching.
Without warning, the partner drops it. Catch it as fast as you can. Read the inches where you caught it. Fewer inches means a faster reaction.
Do 3 tries each. The Recorder writes every result.
Find each person's best try. Graph everyone's best try.
Try again after 1 minute of square breathing. Did it change? Scientists report results either way.
talk: Did reaction times get better with practice?
How did you feel after square breathing?
Where do people need fast reactions in real life?
nights.safety: Drop the ruler straight down from a small height, and keep faces clear. Anyone who feels dizzy during breathing stops and breathes normally.
